explanation: Regular Simple Past: base + -ed. Spelling: double consonant after short vowel (stop → stopped). Drop -e before -ed (like → liked). Change -y to -ied (study → studied). Same form for all persons.
options: Add -s to the base form: walk → walks, play → plays, want → wants
Add -ed to the base form: walk → walked, play → played, want → wanted
Use did + base form: walk → did walk, play → did play, want → did want
Change the stem vowel: sing → sang, drink → drank, swim → swam
question: How is the Simple Past of regular verbs formed?

explanation: Negative: subject + did not + base form. "She didn't come." NOT "She didn't came." Did = auxiliary, so main verb stays in base form. Exception: be → was/were not (no did).
options: Put not after the main verb: She went not. He knew not.
Use did not (didn't) + base form: She didn't go. He didn't know.
Use have not (haven't) + past participle: She hasn't gone. He hasn't known.
Use was/were not + verb-ing: She wasn't going. He wasn't knowing.
question: How do you form the negative in Simple Past?

explanation: Simple Past questions: Did + subject + base form. "Did he call?" NOT "Did he called?" Exception: be → Was/Were + subject. "Was she there?" Short answers: Yes, she did. / No, she didn't.
options: Did + subject + base form: Did she go? Did you see it?
Main verb first + subject: Went she? Saw you it?
Was/were + subject + verb-ing: Was she going? Were you seeing it?
Subject + past form + question mark: She went? You saw it?
question: How do you form questions in Simple Past?

explanation: Irregular verbs: go→went, come→came, see→saw, say→said, get→got, make→made, know→knew, think→thought, take→took, give→gave. Must be learned by heart.
options: Goed
Went
Goes
Gone
question: What is the Simple Past of "go"?

explanation: Simple Past: completed past action. "I visited Paris last year." Signal words: yesterday, last (night/week/year), in 2020, two days ago, when I was young. Compare: Present Perfect (no specific time mentioned).
options: For repeated habits in the present, with signal words like always, often, every day
For finished actions at a fixed time in the past, with signal words like yesterday, last week, ago
For actions in progress in the past, with signal words like while, as, at that moment
For plans and intentions in the future, with signal words like tomorrow, next week, soon
question: When do we use the Simple Past?

explanation: Be: was (singular: I, he, she, it) / were (plural: you, we, they). "I was happy." "They were late." Questions: "Was he there?" "Were you ready?" Negative: wasn't / weren't.
options: Was for all persons: I was, you was, he was, we was, they was
Was for I/he/she/it and were for you/we/they: I was, they were
Were for all persons: I were, you were, he were, we were, they were
Was for the plural and were for the singular: I were, he were, we was
question: What are the forms of "to be" in Simple Past?

explanation: Past Progressive: was/were + -ing. "I was sleeping at 10 pm." Interrupted action: "While I was cooking, she called." Contrast: Simple Past (short completed) vs. Past Progressive (longer background action).
options: A short, completed action in the past, formed with the past form of the verb
An action in progress at a moment in the past, formed with was/were + verb-ing
An action planned for a later time, formed with will + be + verb-ing
An action happening at this very moment, formed with am/is/are + verb-ing
question: What is the Past Progressive (Past Continuous)?

explanation: Present Perfect: have/has + past participle (3rd form). "I have eaten." "She has visited." Past participle: regular (-ed) or irregular (go→gone, see→seen, eat→eaten). No specific time signal.
options: did + past participle: I did seen, she did gone, we did finished
have/has + past participle: I have seen, she has gone, we have finished
was/were + verb-ing: I was seeing, she was going, we were finishing
will + base form: I will see, she will go, we will finish
question: How is the Present Perfect formed?

explanation: SP: "I saw her yesterday." (specific time). PP: "I have seen her before." (no specific time, experience). Signal words: SP (yesterday, last year, ago, in 2010); PP (ever, never, already, just, yet, since, for).
options: Simple Past is used in writing, Present Perfect is used only in spoken language
Simple Past: finished action at a stated time. Present Perfect: relevance now or no stated time
Simple Past: relevance for now. Present Perfect: finished action at a clearly stated time
Simple Past is used with irregular verbs, Present Perfect only with regular verbs
question: What is the difference between Simple Past and Present Perfect?

explanation: Short (1-2 syllables): -er/-est: tall→taller→tallest. Spelling: double consonant (big→bigger), -y→-ier (happy→happier). Long: more/most. Irregular: good→better→best, bad→worse→worst, far→further→furthest.
options: Add -er/-est to every adjective: beautiful → beautifuler → beautifulest, big → bigger
Add -er/-est to short adjectives and more/most to long ones: bigger → biggest, more beautiful
Add more/most to every adjective: more big → most big, more beautiful → most beautiful
Add more/most to short adjectives and -er/-est to long ones: more big, beautifuler
question: What are comparative and superlative forms of adjectives?

explanation: Type 1 conditional: possible situation. "If I study hard, I will pass the exam." If-clause: Simple Present. Main clause: will + base form. Can use other modals: "If it rains, we can/might/should stay inside."
options: An unreal condition now: If + Simple Past, would + base form (If I had time, I would come)
A real or possible condition: If + Simple Present, will + base form (If it rains, I will stay)
An impossible past condition: If + Past Perfect, would have + participle (If I had known)
A general truth: If + Simple Present, Simple Present (If you heat water, it boils)
question: What is an if-clause type 1?

explanation: Much + uncountable: much money, much information, much homework. Many + countable (plural): many cars, many students, many ideas. In positive sentences: a lot of (both). Much/many mainly in negatives/questions.
options: Much with countable nouns (much books), many with uncountable nouns (many water)
Much with uncountable nouns (much water), many with countable nouns (many books)
Much with plural nouns (much cars), many with singular nouns (many car, many idea)
Much in questions only (How much?), many in statements only (I have many)
question: What is the difference between "much" and "many"?

explanation: "Used to": past habit/state, no longer true now. "I used to play football." (but I don't anymore). Questions: "Did you use to...?" Negative: "I didn't use to..." Compare: "would" (past habit, not state).
options: A habit that is still true today: I used to live in Berlin and I still live there
A habit or state in the past that is over: I used to live in Berlin, but not anymore
An intention for the future: I used to move to Berlin at the end of next year
An ability in the past, like could: I used to swim very well when I was a child
question: What does "used to" express?

explanation: Modals: always + base form (no -s, no -ed). Can (ability/permission): I can swim. Must (obligation): You must stop. Should (advice): You should eat well. May/might (possibility). Could (past ability/polite request).
options: Verbs that name a concrete action: run, eat, write, build, speak, work, play
Auxiliary verbs for ability, permission or obligation: can, must, should, may, might
Verbs with irregular past forms: go/went, see/saw, take/took, know/knew, give/gave
Verbs that link subject and complement: be, seem, become, look, feel, sound
question: What are modal verbs in English?

explanation: Can: present (I can speak German). Could: past ability (I could run fast as a child). Polite request: "Could you open the door?" Possibility: "It could rain." Could = more polite/tentative than can.
options: Both express present ability in exactly the same way and can always be swapped
Can: ability or permission now. Could: past ability, polite request or possibility
Can: ability in the past. Could: ability and permission in the present moment
Can: used in questions only. Could: used in statements and short answers only
question: What is the difference between "can" and "could"?

explanation: Passive: be + past participle. Active: "They built the bridge." Passive: "The bridge was built (by them)." Tenses: is written (present), was written (past), has been written (PP), will be written (future).
options: The subject does the action itself: She wrote the book, formed with the normal past form
The object becomes the subject: The book was written by her, formed with be + participle
The action is shown as ongoing: She was writing the book, formed with be + verb-ing
The action is put into the perfect: She has written the book, formed with have + participle
question: What is the passive voice in English?

explanation: Relative pronouns: who (people), which (things), that (both, informal). "The book that/which I read was great." "The woman who/that called is my teacher." Whose (possession): "The student whose bag I found..."
options: Clauses that stand alone as full sentences: The man lives there. He is my uncle.
Clauses that describe a noun with who, which or that: The man who lives there is my uncle.
Clauses that state a condition with if or unless: If the man lives there, he is my uncle.
Clauses that give time or reason with when or because: He is my uncle because he lives there.
question: What are relative clauses in English?

explanation: Gerund: verb-ing as noun. Subject: "Swimming is healthy." After certain verbs: enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, suggest, keep + gerund. "I enjoy swimming." After prepositions: "I'm good at cooking."
options: The -ing form after be, showing an action in progress: She is swimming at the moment.
The -ing form used as a noun, as subject or object: Swimming is fun. I enjoy reading.
The base form with to, used after want or hope: I want to swim. I hope to read a lot.
The third form of the verb, used after have or be: I have swum. The book was read.
question: What is the gerund in English?

explanation: To + infinitive: want to go, decide to stay, hope to win. Purpose: "I study to learn." After adjectives: "glad to help." Modal verbs: no to (can do, must go, should eat). Gerund vs. infinitive: different verbs.
options: After modal verbs such as can, must and should: I can to swim, she must to go home
After verbs like want or decide, after adjectives, and for purpose: I went there to buy milk
After prepositions such as at, of and about: I am good at to cook, afraid of to fall
After verbs like enjoy, avoid and finish: I enjoy to swim, she avoids to run in the rain
question: What is the infinitive with "to" used for?

explanation: "I have lived here since 2015." (point of start). "I have lived here for 8 years." (duration). Since + point: Monday, January, 2010, I was a child. For + period: two hours, a long time, ages, three weeks.
options: Both name the length of a period of time and can be used in exactly the same way
Since names the starting point (since 2020, since Monday), for names the duration (for three years)
Since names the duration (since three years), for names the starting point (for Monday)
Since is used with countable periods, for is used with uncountable periods of time
question: What does "since" vs "for" express with Present Perfect?

explanation: Must-know irregulars: be/was/were/been, have/had/had, do/did/done, go/went/gone, come/came/come, see/saw/seen, give/gave/given, take/took/taken, write/wrote/written, speak/spoke/spoken.
options: goed, comed, seed, doed, haved, sayed, getted, maked, knowed, taked
go/went/gone, see/saw/seen, do/did/done, have/had/had, take/took/taken, know/knew/known
be/was/been is the single irregular verb; all other verbs follow the -ed pattern
walk/walked/walked, play/played/played, want/wanted/wanted, live/lived/lived
question: What are the most common irregular verbs students should know?

explanation: Reported speech: "I am tired" → She said (that) she was tired. Tense shift: present→past, past→past perfect, will→would. Pronouns change. Time/place expressions change (here→there, now→then, today→that day).
options: Repeating the exact words of a speaker in quotation marks: She said, "I am tired."
Telling what someone said without the exact words: She said (that) she was tired.
Turning a statement into a question about the words used: What did she say to you?
Writing a dialogue with a new line for every speaker: – I am tired. – Me too.
question: What is reported speech (indirect speech)?

explanation: Frequency adverbs: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, seldom, never. Position: before main verb ("I always eat breakfast"), after "be" ("She is always late"). "Do you ever...?" "I have never been..."
options: A word that describes a noun more closely: a red car, an old house, three books
A word that tells how often something happens: always, usually, often, sometimes, never
A word that makes an adjective stronger or weaker: very good, quite old, rather cold
A word that says where or when an action happens: here, outside, yesterday, soon
question: What is an adverb of frequency?

explanation: Wh-questions: Who, What, Where, When, Why, How + auxiliary + subject + base form. "Where did you go?" "What does she want?" Exception: who/what as subject: "Who called?" (no auxiliary needed).
options: Question word + subject + main verb: Where you went? What you have eaten?
Question word + auxiliary + subject + base form: Where did you go? What have you eaten?
Question word + main verb + subject: Where went you? What ate you yesterday?
Subject + verb with the question word at the end: You went where? She is crying why?
question: What is the structure of a question with a question word?

explanation: PP relevance: "I have lost my key." (it's still lost, affects now). SP: "I lost my key yesterday." (completed fact). Experience: "Have you ever been to Italy?" Action just completed: "She has just finished." Unfinished: "I have lived here for 5 years."
options: It is the more formal version of the Simple Past, used mainly in written texts
It links the past to the present: experience, recent action, unfinished period of time
It is the more polite form, used for requests and in everyday spoken conversation
It describes actions that lie further back in the past than the Simple Past does
question: What does the Present Perfect express that is different from Simple Past?

explanation: a/an = indefinite article. a + consonant sound: a book, a European (sounds like "Yuropean"). an + vowel sound: an apple, an elephant, an hour, an honest man. It is about the sound, not the spelling.
options: A stands before countable nouns (a car), an before uncountable nouns (an water)
A stands before consonant sounds (a car, a university), an before vowel sounds (an apple, an hour)
A stands before singular nouns (a car), an before plural nouns (an cars, an apples)
A stands before short words (a car), an before longer words (an bicycle, an teacher)
question: What is the difference between "a" and "an"?

explanation: Time prepositions: at (exact time: at 3pm, at midnight, at Christmas). on (specific day/date: on Monday, on my birthday, on 5th June). in (longer period: in the morning, in July, in 2020, in winter).
options: At for days and dates, on for exact times, in for months: at Monday, on 5pm, in July
At for exact times (at 5pm), on for days and dates (on Monday), in for longer periods (in July)
In for exact times, at for months and years, on for seasons: in 5pm, at July, on summer
At for every time expression: at 5pm, at Monday, at July, at 2020, at summer
question: What are prepositions of time in English?

explanation: Place: in (3D space: in the room), on (surface: on the shelf), at (point/place: at home, at the bus stop). Under/below, over/above, next to, beside, between (two things), among (many things).
options: In for surfaces, on for closed spaces, at for larger areas: in the table, on the box
In for closed spaces (in the box), on for surfaces (on the table), at for points (at the door)
On for closed spaces, at for surfaces, in for exact points: on the box, at the table, in the door
At for every place expression: at the box, at the table, at the door, at the shelf
question: What are prepositions of place in English?

explanation: Make: something new is created. Make a phone call, make dinner, make friends, make a plan. Do: activity without producing something tangible. Do sport, do business, do a favour, do your best. Fixed expressions!
options: Both verbs mean the same and can be used in every fixed expression alike
Make for creating something (make a cake, a decision), do for activities (do homework, sport)
Make for activities (make homework, make sport), do for creating something (do a cake)
Make is used in questions and do in statements, otherwise the meaning is the same
question: What is the difference between "make" and "do" in English?

explanation: "There is/are" = existential. There is a problem. (singular). There are many people. (plural). Past: There was/were. Question: Is there...? Are there...? Negative: There isn't/aren't. Used to introduce new info.
options: Another way of saying "it is", with exactly the same meaning: There is cold today.
A way of saying that something exists: there is + singular, there are + plural nouns.
An expression pointing to a place far from the speaker: There is the house over there.
An expression used with the definite article: There is the cat. There are the three cats.
question: What is "there is / there are"?

explanation: Time connectors: First → Then → After that → Finally (sequence). When (at the same time/after). While (simultaneous). Before/After (order). As soon as (immediately). Until (up to a point). During (throughout).
options: And, but, or, as well as – they add information or set two ideas against each other
First, then, after that, finally, when, while, before, after, as soon as, until
Because, so, therefore, although, however – they give reasons, results or contrast
Who, which, that, whose – they attach a description to a noun in the sentence
question: What are the most important time connectors in English?

explanation: -ing spelling: simple: walk→walking, play→playing. Double consonant: short stressed vowel + single consonant: sit→sitting, stop→stopping. Drop -e: make→making, write→writing. -ie→-y: lie→lying, die→dying.
options: Add -ing to the base form unchanged: ride → rideing, swim → swiming, lie → lieing
Double the consonant after a short vowel (swim → swimming), drop silent -e (ride → riding)
Double the final consonant in every verb: walk → walkking, ride → ridding, play → playying
Change every final -y to -ie before -ing: play → plaieing, study → studieing, try → trieing
question: What is the rule for spelling -ing forms?

explanation: False friends: Gift (EN: present, DE: Geschenk/Gift=Poison). Become (EN: werden, DE: bekommen=receive). Sympathetic (EN: mitfühlend, DE: sympathisch=likeable). Art (EN: Kunst, DE: Art=type). Chef (EN: Küchenchef, DE: Chef=boss).
options: Words of both languages that rhyme with each other: house/Haus, mouse/Maus, garden/Garten
Words that look alike but mean different things: gift (Geschenk) vs. Gift (Poison), become vs. bekommen
Words that English has taken from German unchanged: kindergarten, rucksack, hamburger
Words with the same meaning inside one language: big and large, start and begin
question: What are "false friends" between German and English?

explanation: Imperative: base form, no subject. "Open the window." "Don't run." Polite: "Please be quiet." "Could you...?" The subject (you) is understood. For emphasis: "Do sit down!" (emphatic do).
options: The question form of the verb: Do you go? Are you listening carefully to me?
The base form used for orders and requests: Go! Listen carefully! Please sit down.
The past form used to report an order: He went. She listened carefully to the teacher.
Subject + will used for promises: You will go. You will listen carefully to me.
question: What is the imperative in English?

explanation: British vs American: Spelling: -our/-or (colour/color), -re/-er (centre/center), -ise/-ize. Vocab: lorry/truck, biscuit/cookie, chemist/drugstore, post/mail. Present Perfect (BrE) vs Simple Past (AmE) for recent actions.
options: The spelling differs (colour/color), while vocabulary, grammar and sound are identical
Spelling, vocabulary, pronunciation and a few grammar points differ: colour/color, lift/elevator
The pronunciation differs, while spelling, vocabulary and grammar follow the same rules
The vocabulary differs (lift/elevator), while spelling and pronunciation stay the same
question: What are the main differences between British and American English?

explanation: Correlative conjunctions: Both A and B (A und B). Either A or B (entweder A oder B). Neither A nor B (weder A noch B). "Both cats and dogs are popular pets." "Either you study or you fail." "Neither she nor I knew."
options: Both...and excludes two things, either...or includes both, neither...nor offers a choice
Both...and includes two things, either...or offers one of two, neither...nor excludes both
All three connect events in time, like before, after and as soon as in a sentence
All three introduce a condition, like if, unless and provided that in a sentence
question: What does "both ... and", "either ... or", "neither ... nor" express?

explanation: Phrasal verbs: verb + particle = new meaning. Give up (quit), look forward to (sich freuen auf), put off (verschieben), get on with (auskommen), run out of (ausgehen). Very common in English, must be learned.
options: A verb with an unusually large number of letters: understand, congratulate, remember
A verb plus a particle with a new meaning: give up, look after, turn off, find out
A verb that is followed by an auxiliary: can go, must stay, should wait, will come
A verb that forms its past tense with -ed: walked, played, wanted, lived, worked
question: What is a phrasal verb?

explanation: "Say" + (that) + clause: He said (that) he was tired. "Tell" + person + (that) + clause: He told me (that) he was tired. Tell sb: tell me, tell him, tell the class. Common mistake: "He said me" (wrong) → "He told me" (correct).
options: Both verbs work alike and can be used with or without a person as object
Say works without naming the listener (She said it was cold), tell needs a person (She told me)
Say needs a person as object (She said me), tell works without a listener (She told it was cold)
Say is used in questions and tell in statements, otherwise the meaning is the same
question: What is the difference between "say" and "tell"?

explanation: See: involuntary or ability (I see a bird, can you see it?). Look (at): deliberate direction of gaze (look at the map). Watch: follow a moving thing over time (watch the film, watch the children play). Similar: hear/listen to.
options: The three verbs mean the same and can replace each other in every sentence
See: perceive without effort. Look at: direct the gaze on purpose. Watch: follow something moving
See: follow something moving. Look at: perceive without effort. Watch: direct the gaze briefly
See is used for people, look for objects and watch for places, buildings and rooms
question: What is the difference between "look", "see", and "watch"?

explanation: A/an: first mention ("I saw a dog."). The: second mention or unique thing ("The dog was huge.", "the sun", "the Queen"). No article: general statements ("Dogs are friendly.", "I love music."). Tricky: "the" with superlatives, "the Rhine".
options: Short words placed before a noun to show its case: of, to, with, from, by
A/an introduces something new, the points to something known, no article in a general sense
Short words that stand in for a noun in the sentence: he, she, it, they, them
Short words that describe a noun more closely: big, red, old, beautiful, heavy
question: What are articles (definite and indefinite) in English?
